Chapter 4 Chickenpox Time Series knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE) # Suppress warnings 4.1 Introduction Treatment of chickenpox (varicella) cases uses up significant economic resources in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities were interested in the past in determining whether widespread distribution of a chickenpox vaccine would be appropriate (Meszner, Molnar, Rampakakis, Yang, Kuter, & Lara, 2017). The data used for this project are 521 weekly Hungarian chickenpox case counts by county from 2005 to 2014 inclusive, with Budapest regarded as its own administrative region. This data were provided publicly by Rozemberczki, Scherer, Kiss, Sarkar, and Ferenci (2021) and downloaded from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (University of California, 2021). The decision to make vaccines publicly available was already approved in 2018 (“Hungary to provide chickenpox vaccine”, 2018). Nevertheless, the data set may still be able to provide additional insights. My research question is to study whether population density plays a role in the behaviour of the time series. I am interested in whether higher population density may result in a greater number of “super-spreader” events. One key factor will be seasonality in the data set, as it is thought that that colder seasons and the timing of the school year have a significant effect on chickenpox cases (Rozemberczki et al., 2021). This may have different effects in the regions of differing population density. A natural choice in answering this research question is to fit multiplicative seasonal ARIMA models to the chickenpox case numbers, as we can study both seasonality and the case-number dependence on previous values and forecast errors. We will do so for four chosen Hungarian regions. 4.2 Exploratory data analysis Administratively, Hungary is split up into its counties, while the capital city, Budapest, is given a separate designation. Budapest which has, by far, the highest population density in the data set, was an obvious choice to include in my study. Of the remaining data sets, I have chosen the counties with the highest, median and lowest population densities, which are Pest, Heves and Somogy respectively (Hungarian Central Statistical Office, 2019). On a technical note, I chose to aggregate the weekly data into monthly data. The interface used to write in R is RStudio (RStudio Team, 2021). The Stan programming language is indirectly used (Carpenter et al., 2017). Please see Appendices 1 and 2 for R packages used and R code respectively. The aggregation into monthly data was done computationally using the fpp3 package in R, which automatically loads some packages in the tidyverse collection of packages (Hyndman, 2021). This reduces the number of observations to 120 months’ worth of case counts, of which we will take 108 as training data and 12 as test data. Finally, as discussed in Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), fpp3 is used to determine the value for \(\lambda\) in a Box-Cox transformation, in order to adjust for heteroskedasticity in the time series. Assuming the untransformed monthly series is \((x_t)\), this transformation is achieved for non-zero \(\lambda\) via the formula \(y_t = (x_t^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\). Central to our methodology is the R package bayesforecast, which interfaces with the programming language Stan, to fit Bayesian time series models (Alonzo & Cruz, 2020). 4.3.2 Order selection bayesforecast used for ARIMA order selection, the algorithm for which is described below. Note that the process compares the BIC of frequentist fittings to find the preferred order. Firstly, the following constraints are made for a multiplicative seasonal ARIMA model \[ y_t \sim SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12} \] \(p + q + P + Q \leq 6\) \(d + D \leq 2\) \(0 \leq p \leq 5, 0 \leq d \leq 2, 0 \leq q \leq 5\) \(0 \leq P \leq 2, 0 \leq D \leq 2, 0 \leq Q \leq 2\) Steps for model selection, with exhaustive search and approximations off (stepwise=FALSE,approximation=FALSE), are based on the algorithm by Hyndman and Khandakar (2008). The first two steps are used to ensure stationarity. Use Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin test(s) to determine \(d\). Use the period of an STL decomposition to determine \(D\). Exhaustively check the BIC of all possible models within the constraints to determine the preferred \({p,d,q,P,D,Q}\). 4.3.3 Prior and posterior distributions 4.3.3.1 Sampling model As previously, take \((x_t)\) as the untransformed monthly series. For our posterior predictive checks, we will use the Arima function from the forecast package to simulate seasonal ARIMA models with fixed coefficient values. Our main test statistic will be to compare the model, which used 108 observations, to compare to the full set of 120 observations by simulating 120 observations. Two other test statistics will be used – the ACF and PACF of the 120 observations, as these describe the dependence structure of the time series. These posterior checks will be conducted against the original data set, aggregated to monthly data, i.e. prior to the Box-Cox transformation, and with the estimated mean parameter subtracted. The algorithm for posterior predictive draws will work as follows. For 1,000 loops: From the post burn-in set of \(\mathbf{\gamma}\) values, draw a particular row from the coefficient matrix (i.e. parameters from the same iteration). Use the Arima function to simulate the appropriate ARIMA model with coefficients fixed to those that were drawn in step 1. Calculate the test statistics for these simulations. Calculate the proportion of times whether the test statistics exceed the statistics from the real data set. Note that the Heves and Somogy series, exhibit some instabilities when trying to simulate observations, possibly due to the MA or seasonal MA coefficients being close to non-invertible. This is easily fixed by settings a ‘while’ loop to keep simulating until there are no NA values. It should be noted that the Pest series had one seasonal MA coefficient, but did not require this adjustment. 4.4 Results 4.4.1 Convergence and posterior predictive checks Note that even though \(\epsilon\) is part of our sampling model, it is not a parameter of interest since its expected value is fixed at 0, so we ignore it for our convergence checks. Chapter 5 5.0 Conclusion My research question involved looking into the way population density affects the behaviour of chickenpox cases in Hungary. Four time series were chosen that were the farthest apart from each other in terms of population density. Although we only studied a small number of time series, we did see that there was a clear difference in the order of ARIMA fitted moving from the highest population density series to the lowest population density series. This difference can be described as a shift from seasonal and non-seasonal AR coefficients to seasonal and non-seasonal MA coefficients. In other words, in our small sample, for higher population density regions, chickenpox cases were more dependent on chickenpox cases in previous periods or the same month in previous years, while the numbers for lower population regions were more dependent on seasonal and non-seasonal forecast errors. Seasonality, particularly the timing of school holidays, played a significant role in determining this effect. One of the strengths of our analysis is that the ARIMA model fitting was Bayesian. Although we did not have a small data set, adapting the method used in this project for a much shorter time series would not be difficult and the results would likely be robust due to the structure provided by the prior distributions. There are some limitations in this analysis. There appeared to be an issue in simulating some (but not all) series with MA parameters. This was easily fixed by repeatedly simulating until there are no NA values, but may indicate some other issues with my code. If I had more time, I would program my own ARIMA evaluation function rather than using the forecast package. There are several extensions that could be suggested for this analysis. Though once the order was determined, we used a Bayesian method to fit the ARIMA model, the actual process for order selection was frequentist. In other words, the process exhaustively fitted models using frequentist estimation and compared the BIC of these values. It would be easy in principle to replace the frequentist estimation with Bayesian estimation, but this would be very time-consuming to run. Other model selection criteria could be used too, such as leave-one-out cross-validation. There appeared to be a slight misfit for the Pest series in terms of forecast accuracy and residual checks. However, the ARIMA order was determined exhaustively using a frequentist method. It may be beneficial to investigate alternative orders to see if the Bayesian fitting could be improved. Finally, another obvious extension is to study more than one series simultaneously using a vector autoregressive method or a hierarchical method.
